idiom_name: no realization - asyncio/selectors give one permanent leader per process
alternative: one asyncio (or selectors-based) event loop per process; asyncio.to_thread / run_in_executor for blocking calls; ProcessPoolExecutor or multiple processes for CPU-bound work - not a thread pool that takes turns in select()
implementation_notes: The demultiplexer is present - selectors.DefaultSelector picks epoll/kqueue and BaseSelector.select() is the readiness wait - but the pattern's payoff is not: on most builds of CPython only one OS thread at a time can hold an attached thread state because of the GIL, so several threads rotating the leader role cannot process Python-level work in parallel. What remains is a token protocol around a call that already releases the GIL: cost without the benefit. asyncio already encodes the sensible arrangement - the loop's thread is the permanent leader and blocking work is pushed out with asyncio.to_thread/run_in_executor - which is exactly the layering a hand-written pool would re-create, minus the protocol bugs.
code_sketch:
# the loop thread is the permanent leader; handlers interleave, not run in parallel
async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle_client, "127.0.0.1", 8080)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()

async def handle_client(reader, writer):
    data = await reader.read(4096)
    await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_transform, data)  # never block the leader
    writer.write(data); await writer.drain()
pitfalls: A blocking call inside a coroutine blocks the single leader and every socket it demultiplexes; offload with asyncio.to_thread or loop.run_in_executor.
Sending CPU-bound work to a thread pool gains nothing under the GIL - use ProcessPoolExecutor or several processes.
Free-threaded builds remove the GIL but not the design constraint: asyncio still owns the readiness loop and there is no user-visible handle set to share, so the advice is unchanged.
Abandoned (reader, writer) pairs leak transports and descriptors; close them explicitly on every exit path.
